intro.why: The gap between a working notebook and a working product is where most ML projects stall. Seeing the model as one component in a system explains why the rest of this subject (requirements, architecture, testing, deployment) exists.

sections.title: From research idea to production: a transcription start-up
sections.plain: A great model is the easy part; latency, cost, product, pipelines and fairness are the hard parts.
sections.body:
Idea. A researcher builds domain-specific speech-recognition models with transfer learning that work well on medical conversations, academic talks and technical meetups. Manual transcription costs about $1.50 per minute and is slow, and generic tools handle technical vocabulary poorly. So she launches a start-up for affordable transcription and live captioning.

Challenge typeWhat goes wrong
Real-world dataNoisy audio lowers accuracy
PerformanceCustomers expect results within minutes; live captioning needs near real-time
CostCloud compute for training and inference, LLM APIs and GPUs are expensive
Scalability and pricingBalancing speed, cost and quality while staying profitable
Product ecosystemWebsite, backend, payment integration
PipelineManual retraining, fragile workflows, outdated libraries, model updates causing outages
TeamCommunication gaps between ML and engineering
Monitoring and fairnessLittle visibility into live performance; bias and critical errors (medical terms, dialects)

Key takeaway: moving from research prototype to production system requires significant engineering beyond ML.

sections.title: ML model vs ML system
sections.plain: The notebook is a component; the photo app with users, payments and monitoring is the system.
sections.body:
ML model: e.g. an object-detection model in a notebook: data in, predictions out. ML system: e.g. a photo-gallery app: user interface, user management, photo upload, payment, the object-detection model, a database, cloud processing, logging and monitoring.

ViewImproves…To achieve…
Model-centricAlgorithms, features, hyperparametersBetter accuracy
System-centricData, infrastructure, deployment, user experience end to endReliable real-world performance

sections.title: The ML pipeline in production, and hidden technical debt
sections.plain: Courses teach collect → train → evaluate; production adds monitoring, data selection and regular updates.
sections.body:
A full pipeline: model requirements → data collection → cleaning → labelling → feature engineering → training → evaluation → deployment → monitoring, with feedback loops. A typical ML course covers only the middle (building models from given data and evaluating accuracy).

Static (course)In production
Get labelled data (collection, cleaning, labelling)
Identify and extract features
Split into training and evaluation sets
Learn the model from training data
Evaluate on evaluation data
Repeat, revising features		Evaluate the model on production data; monitor it
Select production data for retraining
Update the model regularly (deployment)

Hidden technical debt (Sculley et al., NeurIPS 2015): in real systems, the ML code is a small box surrounded by configuration, data collection, feature extraction, data verification, machine resource management, analysis tools, process management tools, serving infrastructure and monitoring. Each of these is software that must be built, tested and maintained, and most production incidents come from them.

sections.title: ML and non-ML components
sections.plain: ML can be the core of the product or an add-on, and real systems often contain many models.
sections.body:
ExampleRole of ML
Transcription serviceCore: speech recognition is the product
Tax softwareAuxiliary: audit-risk prediction is an add-on to a rule-based product

In both cases ML is a component inside a system of non-ML components (UI, business logic, storage, payments). Large systems contain many ML components and supporting ML infrastructure: in the photo-gallery example, an internal labelling tool, model inference service, feature store, training-data store, ML pipeline, model monitor and telemetry, alongside the product's ordinary services.

Design implications: define interfaces between ML and non-ML parts, decide where ML output is trusted, and handle the case where the ML component is unavailable or wrong.

sections.title: Experiment-driven data development and systems thinking
sections.plain: A data-science track runs alongside the software track and joins it at integration.
sections.body:
Two tracks. The software-engineering process runs requirements → specification and design → implementation → system test → operation. Alongside it, experiment-driven data development (EDDA) runs: is ML suitable? → model requirements → data exploration and model development (iterative experiments) → model integration → operation. The tracks meet at design (model requirements feed the system design), integration and operation.

Systems thinking: understand the system's needs, goals and interactions with its environment; design components and integrate ML and non-ML parts; work across many roles and stakeholders.

What to do when the ML component makes a mistake? Model errors propagate to other components and to the environment (users, physical world). The system must contain them: confidence thresholds, human review, fallbacks to rules, guardrails, undo, monitoring. Code example ex2 quantifies the trade-off: with 1,000 tags from a calibrated model (84.1% accurate), a 0.75 review threshold cuts wrong tags shown to users from 159 to 82 at the cost of 229 human reviews (≈1.9 hours); a 0.90 threshold leaves 20 wrong tags but needs 682 reviews.

sections.title: Predictive, generative and agentic AI
sections.plain: Predict from the past; create new content; pursue goals with reasoning and tools.
sections.body:
ParadigmWhat it doesTypical example
Predictive AIUses past data to predict future outcomesChurn, fraud, demand forecasts
Generative AICreates new content from learned patternsText, images, code drafts
Agentic AIActs autonomously toward goals using reasoning and toolsBook a trip, fix a bug end to end

Generative AI (definition): a system based on a foundation model that generates digital artefacts from natural user instructions. Artefacts range from binary outputs to text, images and video; instructions are easy for humans (everyday language, photos, sketches) and need no technical knowledge.

Agentic AI definitions: "uses sophisticated reasoning and iterative planning to autonomously solve complex, multi-step problems" (Nvidia); "AI systems that can pursue complex goals with limited direct supervision" (OpenAI); and a more formal one: a foundation-model system that performs tasks from natural instructions and can conduct and express complex reasoning, including planning and reflection, for tasks needing interaction with an environment or elaborate tool use.

Generative AI: "Tell me what to do, I'll generate an answer." Agentic AI: "Give me a goal, I'll figure out the steps, act, and improve until it's done." In short: Generative AI + reasoning + tools + feedback loops → agentic AI; the loop resembles reinforcement learning (state, action, reward). Agentic AI is developed further in Session M7.

sections.title: The generative AI stack and its infrastructure needs
sections.plain: Hardware → foundation models → model hubs → hosting/fine-tuning → app frameworks → users.
sections.body:
Layers of a generative AI system: compute hardware (GPU/accelerator vendors) → foundation models (open or proprietary; text, image, video) → model hubs (e.g. Hugging Face) → hosting and fine-tuning services (cloud ML platforms) → application frameworks (LangChain, LlamaIndex, vector databases such as Pinecone or Chroma, UI tools such as Streamlit or Gradio) → end users.

NeedGenerative AIPredictive AI
ComputeExtremely high; specialised hardwareModerate to high; general hardware
DataMassive, diverse datasetsSpecific historical data
TrainingComplex, iterative, specialisedModerate
ScalabilityHighly elasticLower; often batch or event-driven
StorageHigh-performance, diverse, high throughput, low latencyEfficient, moderate, structured
NetworkingHigh bandwidth, low latency (distributed training)Consistent and reliable

sections.title: Cloud-native ML systems
sections.plain: Containers, orchestration and declarative APIs give ML scalable, reliable infrastructure.
sections.body:
AI/ML is a fast-growing cloud workload. The CNCF defines cloud-native technologies as those that "empower organizations to build and run scalable applications in modern, dynamic environments such as public, private, and hybrid clouds. Containers, service meshes, microservices, immutable infrastructure, and declarative APIs exemplify this approach."

Layered view: workloads (predictive and generative) → ML life cycle (data, training, serving) → platform (orchestration and scheduling, e.g. Kubernetes) → infrastructure (public clouds) → hardware (CPU, GPU, TPU, DPU). Different personas (data scientists, ML engineers, platform and infrastructure engineers) own different layers. Containers and Kubernetes are covered in Session M12.

sections.title: Case study: a 28-model autonomous-driving system
sections.plain: Real systems wire many models together with code; failures propagate.
sections.body:
An open autonomous-driving platform (Apollo, by Baidu) is a representative complex ML system. It is not built around one model: multiple ML components interact with traditional software to make real-time driving decisions.

  • Perception: traffic-light detection and recognition (CNNs), lane detection, obstacle detection from cameras (YOLO-style detectors) and LiDAR (CNN segmentation).
  • Prediction: vehicle and pedestrian trajectory prediction (MLPs, CNNs, RNNs/LSTMs).
  • Planning and control: largely code that consumes model outputs.
Seven lessons
  1. ML systems ≠ standalone models: many models plus code logic.
  2. Large-scale ML architecture: 28 models across perception, detection and prediction.
  3. Model interaction is complex: outputs of one model are inputs of others.
  4. Code is critical: pre-processing, post-processing, validation and decision logic.
  5. Multi-source fusion: camera, LiDAR, radar and maps combined.
  6. Scenario-based model selection: different models for different traffic and road conditions.
  7. SE challenges: high complexity, low test coverage, model maintenance, need for system-level quality assurance.

sections.title: Case study: a nine-stage ML workflow and SE practices for ML
sections.plain: Large teams adapt SE practices: data is central, work is iterative, new roles appear.
sections.body:
A study of software teams at Microsoft (Amershi et al., 2019) found that teams build ML systems with adapted engineering practices. It proposes a nine-stage workflow (model requirements, data collection, data cleaning, data labelling, feature engineering, model training, model evaluation, deployment, monitoring) that is highly iterative with feedback loops, places data at the centre (collection, cleaning, labelling and versioning are the hard parts), needs new roles alongside developers, integrates with agile/DevOps, and introduces a process maturity model for ML.

SE practice adopted for MLWhat it means
Agile/DevOps integrationML workflows embedded in continuous development and deployment
End-to-end pipelinesAutomated data, training, evaluation and deployment
Data engineering as core SECollection, cleaning, versioning are engineering tasks, not just preprocessing
Experimentation-driven developmentIterative experiments with models, features and data
Versioning beyond codeModels and datasets versioned with provenance metadata
Continuous evaluation and monitoringMetrics, real-world feedback, human-in-the-loop validation
Model debugging and interpretabilityExplainability and visualisation tools
Cross-functional teamsData scientists, ML engineers, domain experts and developers together
System-level complexityEntangled ML components need system-level testing and integration
Process maturityCMM-like models to assess automation, consistency and improvement

sections.title: Further insights and misconceptions
sections.body:
• "Improve the model and the product improves." Only if the bottleneck is the model; often it is data quality, latency or UX.
  • "Monitoring is optional for good models." Code example ex1: a model trained once falls from 93% to 54% accuracy over twelve months of gradual drift, while a monitored pipeline that retrains on recent data stays between 84% and 93%.
  • "Agentic AI replaces predictive AI." They solve different problems and are often combined (an agent calling a fraud model).
  • "More models means more accuracy." More models also mean more interfaces, more failure propagation and harder testing.

code.title: Static pipeline vs production pipeline under drift
code.explain: Simulates twelve months of gradually drifting customer behaviour. A model trained once is compared with a pipeline that monitors accuracy and retrains on the most recent data when it drops below 90%.
mistakes: Monitoring accuracy without labels: in production you often need delayed ground truth or proxy metrics.
Retraining on all historical data, which keeps old patterns alive.
code.notes: In production the threshold, data window and retraining trigger are configuration that must be versioned and tested.
code.code:
# A static pipeline (train once) vs a production pipeline (monitor, select data, retrain)
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(3)
def batch(month, n=600):
    """Customers whose behaviour drifts: the decision boundary rotates a little each month."""
    X = rng.normal(size=(n, 2))
    angle = 0.12 * month
    w = np.array([np.cos(angle), np.sin(angle)])
    y = (X @ w + 0.3 * rng.normal(size=n) > 0).astype(int)
    return X, y

X0, y0 = batch(0)
static = LogisticRegression().fit(X0, y0)          # trained once, never updated
live = LogisticRegression().fit(X0, y0)            # same start, but maintained
window_X, window_y = [X0], [y0]
print("month  static_acc  production_acc  action")
for m in range(1, 13):
    X, y = batch(m)
    s_acc, p_acc = static.score(X, y), live.score(X, y)
    action = "-"
    if p_acc < 0.90:                                # monitoring threshold
        window_X, window_y = window_X[-2:] + [X], window_y[-2:] + [y]   # select recent data
        live = LogisticRegression().fit(np.vstack(window_X), np.concatenate(window_y))
        action = "retrain on last 3 months"
    else:
        window_X.append(X); window_y.append(y)
    print(f"{m:5d}  {s_acc:10.3f}  {p_acc:14.3f}  {action}")

code.title: Error budget: confidence threshold and human review
code.explain: For 1,000 predictions from a calibrated model, shows how a review threshold trades wrong outputs shown to users against human review effort.
mistakes: Assuming confidences are calibrated without checking (reliability diagrams).
code.notes: The same pattern is used for content moderation, medical triage and document processing.
code.code:
# What the system around a model does with its mistakes: confidence threshold + human review
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
n = 1000
conf = 0.5 + 0.5 * rng.beta(2.5, 1.2, n)        # calibrated confidences
correct = rng.random(n) < conf                    # P(correct) = confidence
print(f"model accuracy: {correct.mean():.3f}  ({(~correct).sum()} wrong tags)")
print("threshold  to_review  wrong_shown  review_hours(30s each)")
for t in [0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, 0.9, 0.95]:
    review = conf < t
    shown_wrong = (~correct & ~review).sum()
    print(f"{t:9.2f}  {review.sum():9d}  {shown_wrong:11d}  {review.sum() * 30 / 3600:8.1f}")
